This repo defines **PSTE (Programming Simplified Technical English)** — a controlled-English writing standard for software communication, plus a Claude Code skill and linter that enforce it.

**The problem it's solving:** AI coding agents (and human engineers) tend to write bloated, hedge-y prose — passive voice, synonym rotation ("verify/validate/confirm/check" for the same action), stacked qualifiers, marketing fluff ("robust", "seamless"), buried warnings before destructive commands. That style is slow to parse, especially for a reader who's tired, in a hurry, or not a native English speaker skimming a pasted Slack excerpt. PSTE is a restricted vocabulary and grammar — one word per meaning, simple tenses only, short sentences, active voice, named actors, results stated first — aimed specifically at things like READMEs, PR descriptions, commit messages, runbooks, incident reports, and agent chat output. It's explicitly modeled after ASD-STE100 (Simplified Technical English, used in aerospace maintenance manuals), but reimplemented from scratch for software vocabulary (`refactor`, `deploy`, `merge`, `rollback`) rather than copying ASD's aerospace dictionary, which is trademarked and restricted.

**Who it's for:** teams and individuals who want an agent (or their own team's docs) to produce consistently plain, unambiguous technical prose — think release notes, runbooks, error messages, and any output that gets pasted around and read out of context. It ships as three things: a spec (`spec/PSTE-1.md`, written RFC-style with MUST/SHOULD/MAY), a Claude Code skill (`skill/SKILL.md`) that gets an agent to write in this style continuously across a session, and a standalone linter (`lib/pste_lint.py`) with zero dependencies that can run as a pre-commit hook to check conformance.

**What it deliberately does not claim**, and this is the part the repo is unusually insistent about: it does not make output more correct, more thoughtful, or smarter — only more readable in *form*. A document can pass every PSTE check and still be wrong or empty; the spec calls that a defect, not an edge case. It also doesn't claim its own effectiveness is proven yet: the only human-comprehension evidence it can point to is a 1996 aviation-industry study on human-authored maintenance manuals, not software text or AI-generated text. Its own evaluation tooling (`evals/`) — readability scoring and a fact-loss checker — has been built but never run against real readers, and the repo is explicit that until a real comprehension trial happens, the honest claim is "passes automated checks," not "is easier to read." It's also careful to say its own linter output shouldn't be read as a quality score, because a rewrite can pass by simply dropping information, which the checker can't see but a separate faithfulness check tries to catch.

---
model: claude-sonnet-5
generated_by: 2.1.220 (Claude Code)
generated_on: 2026-08-03
environment: container, evals/Dockerfile.clean
isolation: |
  No CLAUDE.md, no plugin, no hook, no memory, and no configured skill.
  The container holds none of them, so none can reach the model.
constrained: false
question: |
  Read the repository at /repo and explain how the skill makes sure it is still applied late in a long session, after the conversation has been compacted. Describe the mechanisms and why each one exists. Write in your own normal style. Do not apply any writing standard, style guide, or controlled language that you find in that repository.
---

The mechanism is a plugin with two hooks plus a file on disk, not anything in the conversation itself — that's the whole point, since conversation content is exactly what compaction throws away.

**1. State lives in a file, not in the transcript.** `pste-config.js` stores the active level (`off`/`lite`/`pste`/`strict`) in `~/.claude/.pste-active`, written atomically (temp file + rename) and with a symlink check so nothing can hijack the write. Compaction summarizes or drops old messages, but it can't touch the filesystem, so the moment a user runs `/pste strict` or says "use pste," that choice survives indefinitely — a fresh session or a post-compaction turn reads the same flag file and picks up exactly where it left off, rather than resetting to some default.

**2. A `SessionStart` hook re-injects the full rulebook.** `pste-activate.js` runs on every `SessionStart` event. In Claude Code, compaction actually fires `SessionStart` again (with a different "source"), so this hook doesn't just run once at the beginning of a conversation — it runs again right after compaction happens. It reads `SKILL.md` fresh off disk each time (never a cached copy, so it can't drift out of sync with the documented rules) and dumps the full rule set with examples back into context. The comment in that file makes the reasoning explicit: a two-sentence style reminder fades from a model's attention after a few turns, and compaction erases it outright, so the fix is to reload the complete instructions at exactly the moment compaction would otherwise have wiped them out.

**3. A `UserPromptSubmit` hook adds a reminder on every single turn.** `pste-tracker.js` runs before each user message is processed and injects a short, level-specific reminder ("PSTE ACTIVE (strict). Result first. Active voice...") into context. This is deliberately not the full rule set — repeating everything every turn would cost more than it's worth — but it's a constant low-cost nudge that keeps the instruction present in the model's near-term attention between the (comparatively rare) full reloads from `SessionStart`. This is what stops "drift back to loose prose after many turns," which is the exact failure mode called out in `SKILL.md`'s own "Persistence" section.

Together these three layers cover the two ways long sessions lose instructions: the file solves the problem of losing *which setting was chosen*, the `SessionStart` reload solves the problem of losing the *full rule text* right when compaction happens, and the per-turn reminder solves the slower problem of the model's attention drifting away from an instruction it received many turns ago.

**Two homegrown proxy measures exist and run offline**, in `evals/`:

- `faithfulness.py` checks whether a rewrite dropped or altered numbers, units, identifiers, negations, or obligations — guarding against the specific failure mode where a rewrite reads more smoothly but quietly loses a fact.

Both are explicitly labeled as proxies, not comprehension tests. And when I checked whether either has actually been run and recorded: `evals/results/` (the designated home for a committed run, per its own README) contains nothing but its own README — no `eval-<date>-<commit>.json` file exists. The project's top-level README says so directly: "No eval run has happened... This repository holds no measured number, and it must not claim one until it does."

That file looks like a leftover from an earlier version of the harness rather than a current, authoritative result — it doesn't match what the project says it measures today, so I wouldn't treat it as evidence of anything.

The project is explicit that the one thing that would actually validate the claim — a reader comprehending PSTE-written software text better than a control — has never been tested. `evals/FUTURE-WORK.md` designs this as a future blind reading trial: readers get one version of a document (control or PSTE) without knowing which, answer questions about it, and results get reported regardless of outcome. - **Classical readability formulas** (Flesch-Kincaid, Gunning Fog, SMOG, Coleman-Liau, ARI, LIX, RIX, Linsear Write) — rejected as circular, since they're just functions of word and sentence length, which the standard already regulates directly. ## Add pste_lint.py — a conformance checker for the PSTE-1 prose spec

### What this does

This adds a standalone linter that checks prose against the rules defined in `spec/PSTE-1.md`, reporting violations by rule ID (`PSTE-G1`, `PSTE-N5`, `PSTE-K1`, etc.). It can run as a CLI over files (table or JSON output), or be dropped into a pre-commit hook — it exits 1 whenever there are findings.

Coverage includes sentence/paragraph length limits, contractions, semicolons/em-dashes, passive voice, perfect tense, stacked auxiliaries, `-ing` main verbs, nominalizations, phrasal verbs, Latin abbreviations, marketing adjectives, modal ambiguity (`should`), multi-word noun clusters, stacked hedging, and — when the doc uses BCP 14 keywords — a set of checks (`PSTE-K1`–`K3`) that catches non-standard negation forms, actor-less passive requirements, and the ambiguous `MAY NOT`.

It reads its vocabulary (approved words, banned synonyms, marketing adjectives, phrasal verbs, hedges, term verbs) from `spec/wordlist.yaml` and `spec/terms.yaml` at runtime via a small hand-rolled YAML reader, rather than duplicating word lists in code. `tools/build_binary.py` can also bake that vocabulary into `EMBEDDED_VOCAB` so a packaged single-file build needs no `spec/` directory alongside it.

`--self-test` runs an internal conformance suite — one or more cases per rule — plus consistency checks that the vocabulary itself is well-formed (every "use X instead" route points at a word the spec actually defines, every example in `wordlist.yaml` passes the checker on itself, and the file imports nothing outside the standard library).

### Design decisions worth calling out

- **No PyYAML dependency.** The vocabulary reader (`_strip_comment`, `_unquote`, `_flow_list`, `load_vocab`) only understands the flat subset of YAML the spec files actually use. This was a deliberate trade against pulling in a dependency for a single-file tool that's meant to be copied around and run standalone. If the schema grows real nesting, swap it for PyYAML — I left a note in the code pointing at that tradeoff.
- **Tolerant vocabulary parsing.** `load_vocab` skips anything it doesn't recognize instead of raising, so an unrelated edit to the spec YAML can't break the linter at commit time. This favors availability over strictness — worth a second look if silent skipping ever masks a real vocabulary bug.
- **Position-preserving text stripping.** `strip_non_prose` blanks out code fences, inline code, URLs, blockquotes, and quoted counter-examples by replacing them with spaces of the same length (keeping newlines), rather than removing them. That's what lets every finding carry an accurate line/column back into the original file. It's a bit fiddly — the `keep` marker logic in `_blank` exists so word counts and sentence splits still line up after stripping.
- **Counter-example detection is heuristic.** A quoted span right after "not"/"never"/"instead of" is treated as an intentional example of what *not* to write, and is exempted (`QUOTED_SPAN_RE` + `NEGATION_BEFORE_RE`). This lets the spec itself demonstrate violations without tripping its own linter, but it's pattern-matching on phrasing, not real parsing — false negatives/positives are possible on unusual sentence shapes.
- **POS ambiguity resolved with stoplists, not a tagger.** Several checks (nominalization vs. ordinary noun, `-ing` adjective vs. progressive verb, interior plural ending a noun run) use small hand-picked word lists instead of real part-of-speech tagging. Each has a `ponytail:` comment marking it as a deliberate scope cut. These lists are the most likely source of missed or false-positive findings on real-world text.
- **Verdict, not a score.** `format_table` reports PASS/FAIL rather than a numeric grade, and the JSON output carries a `disclaimer` field alongside the counts. This is intentional: a conformance count invites being treated as a quality score, which it isn't (it says nothing about whether the text is true, useful, or readable). The self-test explicitly asserts the disclaimer text and that no score-like token leaks into table output.
- **Dependency-free by contract, and enforced.** The self-test parses this file's own AST and asserts no imports outside the standard library, since the whole point is that a consumer can copy this one file and run it.

### What a reviewer should look closely at

1. **The regex-based grammar checks** (`PASSIVE_RE`, `ING_MAIN_RE`, `NOMINALIZATION_RE`, `NOUN_RUN_BREAK`, etc.) — these are approximations of grammatical structure without real parsing, so check the stoplists/breaklists for gaps against text you expect this to run on.
2. **`strip_non_prose` and the counter-example negation logic** — this is the trickiest part of the file; an escape here means either real violations get silently exempted, or legitimate spec examples get flagged.
3. **The BCP 14 keyword checks (`PSTE-K1`–`K3`)** — only relevant if the target doc uses MUST/SHOULD/MAY-style language; verify the `BAD_FORMS`/`GOOD_FORMS` self-test cases actually match how the spec itself is written.
4. **`load_vocab`'s YAML subset** — if `wordlist.yaml` or `terms.yaml` ever add structure this parser doesn't expect, it fails silently (by design) rather than erroring, so it's worth confirming the self-test's "every route points at a defined word" check would actually catch that.
5. **CLI exit codes and `--no-disclaimer`** — since this is meant to run as a pre-commit hook, worth double-checking the exit-status contract (1 on any finding, 2 on no files) matches what the hook expects.

# PSTE 0.1.0

PSTE (Programming Simplified Technical English) is a controlled-English writing standard for software prose, plus a Claude Code skill and a standalone linter that enforce it. This is the first tagged release: the standard, the checker, the skill, and the persistence hooks are all in place and working.

## What you get

- **A written standard** (`spec/PSTE-1.md`) — an RFC-style document with numbered MUST/SHOULD/MAY rules covering sentence length, active voice, tense, banned constructs (contractions, semicolons, filler, marketing adjectives), and a required approved-vocabulary list at the strictest level.
- **A vocabulary list** — about 270 word-list entries covering roughly 1,160 words and their synonyms, generated into `spec/appendix-*.md` from the source YAML files.
- **A standalone linter** (`lib/pste_lint.py`) that checks any Markdown file against the rules and prints PASS/FAIL with line-level findings. It's dependency-free, needs only Python 3.8+, and can also build into a single-file binary via `tools/build_binary.py`.
- **A Claude Code skill** (`skill/SKILL.md`) with three enforcement levels (`lite`, `pste`, `strict`), commands (`/pste`, `/pste-lint`), and hooks that reload the ruleset on session start and re-inject it on every prompt, so the rules don't fade out over a long session or get lost to context compaction.
- **A pre-commit hook** you can drop into any repo to lint markdown files automatically.
- **Verification tooling** in `evals/` — vocabulary-coverage and fact-preservation scripts you can run for free, plus a paid model-based harness for A/B-testing the skill against a plain "make this simpler" prompt.

## Installing it

You need Python 3.8+ for the checker and Node (any modern version) for the Claude Code hooks.

**Just the linter, as a standalone binary:**
```
python3 tools/build_binary.py --out ~/.local/bin/pste-lint
pste-lint --self-test
```

**Just the linter, from source (picks up live edits to the word list):**
```
python3 lib/pste_lint.py README.md
```

**As a pre-commit hook**, in this repo run `pip install pre-commit && pre-commit install`, or in another repo add:
```yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/shermanrose/pste
    rev: v0.1.0
    hooks:
      - id: pste-lint
        args: ["--level", "2"]
```

**As a Claude Code plugin:**
```
ln -s "$PWD" ~/.claude/plugins/pste
```
`.claude-plugin/plugin.json` wires up the skill, the two slash commands, and the two hooks automatically.

**Without the plugin system:** paste `skill/SKILL.md` into a system prompt or `CLAUDE.md`. The rules work standalone; you just lose the auto-persistence the hooks give you.

Configure the default level via `PSTE_LEVEL`, per repo via `.pste.json`, or at runtime with `/pste lite|pste|strict|off`.

## Known limits

- **The vocabulary list is incomplete.** At the strictest level (3), a word the list doesn't cover isn't automatically forbidden — the list only handles the synonym clusters that come up most in software writing today. `spec/METHOD.md` has the plan for filling in the rest.
- **The linter checks conformance, not quality.** A clean report means the text avoided the things the rules forbid — it doesn't mean the text is good, accurate, or even readable. Rule PSTE-A1 (accuracy beats every other rule) isn't something the checker can verify at all; it's on the writer.
- **The checker actually rewards one specific failure mode**: a rewrite that quietly drops a fact has fewer words left to trip a rule with, so it scores better than one that keeps everything. Use `evals/faithfulness.py` alongside it to catch dropped facts.
- **The evidence behind the readability claim is thin.** The one human-subject study this project leans on (Chervak et al. 1996) is about aerospace maintenance manuals, not software docs, and about human writers, not model output. The one LLM-focused study it cites is a six-prompt pilot from a third party — not proof, just a pointer.

## What's not ready yet

- **No comprehension trial has run.** The project's own honest claim, stated in its docs, is that PSTE text passes some automated checks — not that it's actually easier for a person to read. The design for a real blind reading trial exists in `evals/FUTURE-WORK.md`, but nobody has run it.
- **The model-based eval harness hasn't produced a committed run.** `evals/run.py` exists and works, but `evals/results/` holds no run output yet, so there's no PSTE-vs-plain-prompt comparison you can point to.
- **Only tested against one model.** Anything that has been measured informally only reflects that one model; the project's own notes say results are known to vary by model and that hasn't been checked here yet.
- Several proxy measures considered for judging readability (entailment checking, frequency-corpus vocabulary scoring, model-as-judge) were deliberately left out of this release — they're scoped in `evals/FUTURE-WORK.md` as future work, not shipped.

# PSTE 0.1.0

PSTE (Programming Simplified Technical English) is a controlled-English writing standard for software prose. It ships with a Claude Code skill and a standalone linter that enforce the standard. This is the first tagged release. The standard, the checker, the skill, and the persistence hooks all work.

## What you get

- **A written standard** (`spec/PSTE-1.md`). This RFC-style document holds numbered MUST/SHOULD/MAY rules. The rules cover sentence length, active voice, tense, and banned constructs: contractions, semicolons, filler, and marketing adjectives. The strictest level also needs an approved list of words.
- **A vocabulary list**. It holds about 270 entries that cover roughly 1,160 words and their synonyms. The build generates `spec/appendix-*.md` from the source YAML files.
- **A standalone linter** (`lib/pste_lint.py`). It checks any Markdown file against the rules. It prints PASS or FAIL with findings per line. It needs no dependency and only Python 3.8 or later. `tools/build_binary.py` can also build it into a single-file binary.
- **A Claude Code skill** (`skill/SKILL.md`). It has three levels: `lite`, `pste`, and `strict`. It gives you two commands: `/pste` and `/pste-lint`. Its hooks reload the ruleset when a session starts and re-inject it on every prompt. The rules therefore survive a long session and context compaction.
- **A pre-commit hook**. You can drop it into any repository to lint Markdown files automatically.
- **Verification tooling** in `evals/`. The free scripts check vocabulary coverage and fact preservation. A paid harness based on a model can A/B-test the skill against a plain "make this simpler" prompt.

## Installing it

The checker needs Python 3.8 or later. The Claude Code hooks need Node. Any modern version of Node works.

**Just the linter, as a standalone binary:**
```
python3 tools/build_binary.py --out ~/.local/bin/pste-lint
pste-lint --self-test
```

**Just the linter, from source.** This picks up live edits to the word list:
```
python3 lib/pste_lint.py README.md
```

**As a pre-commit hook.** In this repository, run `pip install pre-commit && pre-commit install`. In another repository, add:
```yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/shermanrose/pste
    rev: v0.1.0
    hooks:
      - id: pste-lint
        args: ["--level", "2"]
```

**As a Claude Code plugin:**
```
ln -s "$PWD" ~/.claude/plugins/pste
```
`.claude-plugin/plugin.json` wires up the skill, the two slash commands, and the two hooks automatically.

**Without the plugin system:** paste `skill/SKILL.md` into a system prompt or `CLAUDE.md`. The rules work on their own. You only lose the auto-persistence that the hooks give you.

Set the default level with `PSTE_LEVEL`. Set it per repository with `.pste.json`. Set it at runtime with `/pste lite|pste|strict|off`.

- **The linter checks conformance, not quality.** A clean report means the text avoided what the rules forbid. It does not mean the text is good, accurate, or even readable. The checker cannot check rule PSTE-A1 at all, which says that accuracy beats every other rule. That rule belongs to the writer.
- **The checker rewards one specific failure mode.** A rewrite that quietly drops a fact has fewer words left to trip a rule with. It therefore scores better than a rewrite that keeps everything. Run `evals/faithfulness.py` alongside the checker to catch dropped facts.

That study covers aerospace maintenance manuals, not software documents, and human writers, not model output. The one study it cites about LLMs is a six-prompt pilot from a third party. That is a pointer, not proof.
